summary: Martha's Vineyard light lit October 1817 at the west entrance to Vineyard Haven; a brick tower from 1891, automated in 1976, still active. The Coast Guard grounds are closed to visitors.

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds, dwellings and tower closed to visitors. Visible from the road and from ferries bound to and from Woods Hole.

events.note: Land bought for $225 from Abijah and Mary Luce; 25-foot rubblestone tower and stone dwelling built by Duncan McBean
In service October 5, 1817, with ten lamps
Captain James Shaw West hired as first keeper
Lieutenant Edward W. Carpender reports the sea encroaching on the tower and dwelling, and recommends moving the light about 300 yards south if necessary (quoted by LighthouseFriends)
Keeper's account: bluff washed to within 37 feet of the base; 30 feet of bluff lost in one storm (quoted by LighthouseFriends)

New rubble-masonry tower and keeper's house built about 1,000 feet southeast (LighthouseFriends); the 1891 report calls the 1846 tower rubble masonry; the survey form says brick and dates the present location to 1847
Charles West replaces James West; not a son of James
Fog signal building and oil house built (survey form); the fog signal building is dated 1881 by LighthouseFriends
Winslow Lewis reflector system installed
Fourth-order Fresnel lens replaces the reflectors
Charles P. West, son of Charles West, succeeds his father as head keeper
Ten-inch steam fog whistle placed in operation December 1, 1881, in a new frame engine house
Stone dwelling of 1846 torn down; frame dwelling built on its foundation
Light moved to a temporary tower about 60 feet from the old tower, August 20, 1891
Rubble-masonry tower of 1846 demolished; new brick tower, 45 feet high, built on the old foundation
Light transferred to the new brick tower, 17 feet higher than the old one, on December 31, 1891
Oil house built (the survey form dates a brick oil house with slate roof to 1847)
Oil-engine air compressor replaces the steam fog signal (LighthouseFriends; the survey form gives 1933 for a compressor replacing the steam boiler)
Air whistle compressor replaces steam boiler (survey form)
Automated; the last of the Martha's Vineyard lights to lose its resident keeper
Lighthouses of Massachusetts nomination form stamped May 1987; NRHP reference 87001506
President Clinton speaks at the Coast Guard station at West Chop on signing the Oceans Act of 2000, August 7, 2000 per the Presidency Project (LighthouseFriends gives August 8)

notes_for_editor: 1) Tower height: the 1891 Light-House Board report gives 45 feet (13.7 m), LighthouseFriends 45 feet, the survey form 52 feet; the record says 14.0 m. The facts use 13.7 m. 2) The 1846 tower: the Board's 1891 report says rubble masonry; LighthouseFriends says a conical stone tower; the survey form says brick, and gives the present location as 1847 rather than 1846. Not resolved. 3) Fog signal: the survey form dates the fog signal building to 1847 (remodeled 1891); LighthouseFriends dates the engine house for the steam whistle to 1881; the Board's reports show a steam whistle in 1891 and 1899. The record says a horn; the survey form calls it an air whistle. 4) Oil house: the survey form dates the brick oil house with slate roof to 1847 and also lists an 1895 oil house; the Board's 1895 report says an oil house was built that year. Facts use 1895. 5) Dwellings: the survey form says the mirror-image dwellings were built in 1847 and remodeled in 1891, and elsewhere says built or constructed in 1881; LighthouseFriends says a frame dwelling for the head keeper was built in 1881. Facts use 1881. 6) Compressed-air fog signal: LighthouseFriends says 1923; the survey form says 1933. Not resolved. 7) Range: the record gives 14 nm; the 1981 survey form says 15 miles. Not used. 8) Oceans Act signing: LighthouseFriends says August 8, 2000; the Presidency Project remarks are dated August 7 (Monday), and the story uses August 7. 9) Name overlaps: James Yates (also a Nauset head keeper in LighthouseFriends, 1918-1919) and Thomas J. Kelley (also a Nauset head keeper, 1914-1918) share names with West Chop keepers; no source read connects them. 10) The record's ownership is federal; the survey form and LighthouseFriends agree the Coast Guard owns it. 11) The archive's roster spells David A. Lycke; LighthouseFriends spells David L. Lycke. Richard E. Laine follows the archive; LighthouseFriends has a typo. 12) The keeper daughter's book is cited only through LighthouseFriends's quotation; no copy of the book was read. 13) The 1838 and 1843 keeper accounts are cited through LighthouseFriends's quotation; the original reports were not among the sources read. 14) LighthouseFriends is an all-rights-reserved site: facts paraphrased, with short phrases quoted. 15) The record's NRHP listing date is not verified; the nomination form is stamped May 4, 1987. 16) Fact-check 2026-10-22: the USLHS record gives Year Established 1818; LighthouseFriends and the NRHP chronology give 1817 (land bought 15 April 1817, first lit 5 October 1817), so 1817 is used. 17) The 1891-92 Board volume holds two reports; the 1846/1891 tower, the 1891 move (scan 341, 17 feet higher), the whistle hours (scan 395) and the 1846 rubble-masonry description (scan 391) are all in the report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1892. 18) The 1895 oil house and fog-machinery entry (scan 237) is in the report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1895; the 1899 whistle entry (scan 96) is in the report for the fiscal year ended June 30, 1899. 19) The NRHP chronology dates a brick tower to 31 October 1846 but describes a rubble-stone tower of 1847 in its narrative; the story reports both.
